business_type_notes: One GBP category (Scaffolding Service) covers the trade, so every page is type A and category_types is empty. The pack's section 2 splits the one category by service group and the split is carried in the card briefs, not in types: access led (the building and the job, how the scaffold answers it) for scaffold hire, domestic, chimney and commercial scaffolding, cantilever and truss out, birdcage, pavement and road, heritage, suspended access, hoists and loading bays, stair towers, access towers and event scaffolding; protection led (what the weather or a fall would do, why, and what prevents it) for temporary roofs, debris netting and sheeting and edge protection; schedule led (what slips and when) for scaffold inspections and scaffold design. Emergency scaffolding is problem led through the library's emergency column: the emergency variant switches on when the client confirms call outs, and every other page gets the plain briefs. The pack calls nothing desire led (it uses access, protection and schedule led instead), so the library's desire_led column is blank and there is no desire variant: the plain type A block 4 is already written as the customer's situation, never a symptom. Nothing is a recurring round, so there is no type B. Year round and weather led, not seasonal: seasonal_trade is off. The reader is as often the roofer, builder or renderer as the homeowner: every brief carries both readings.

steps.title: Tell Us About the Building and the Job
steps.brief: How to get in touch and what is useful to send first: which trade needs the access and what they are doing (a roof, a chimney, render, windows), which sides of the building and how high, roughly when the trade wants to start, and photos from the street and the garden if they have them. A roofer or builder sends the same in their own words: the elevations, the heights, where the materials will land, the dates. No promise of a reply time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps.title: We Survey and Price the Scaffold
steps.brief: The visit and what gets looked at: what the feet will stand on (lawn, paving, a drive, a drain cover, soft ground), where the ties can go, how the lorry gets in, and whether any of it will stand on the pavement or on next door's side, which is where the council's licence or the neighbour's agreement usually comes in before the start (Table A). Follows [CV: quote_method]; only say the quote is written if quote_method says so. Never restates 'free' (FAQ 5 owns it). No erection time, hire period or price unless the client values give it.

steps.title: We Put It Up for the Date Your Trade Needs It
steps.brief: The date agreed around the other trade's start, so the hire is not running while nobody is on it. The scaffold handed over and checked before anyone climbs it, as the job usually goes (Table A). Never mention the price, the quote or changes to the plan (step 2 and Why choose us own them). Never restates the start time (FAQ 4 owns it). Nothing about how long the build takes unless the client values give it.

step_2_no_visit.title: We Price Your Scaffold
step_2_no_visit.brief: Say a price is agreed before anything goes up. Describe how the price is reached only from [CV: quote_method]; when quote_method is blank, name no method at all (no photos, call, video or visit). Only say the quote is written if quote_method says so. Never restates 'free' (FAQ 5 owns it).

steps_emergency.title: Call Us
steps_emergency.brief: What to say: what has happened (a chimney or a parapet shifted, a roof opened by a storm or a fire, render falling, a scaffold that has moved), where it is, whether it is over a pavement, a drive, a door or a neighbour's garden, and whether people can still get past it. What to do meanwhile, from the trade facts first stage (make the area safe and keep people out of it): keep everyone from under it, including from the pavement where that can be done, keep the children and the car away from it, tell the neighbours whose side it is over, and nobody up a ladder or onto the roof. The number from [CV: phone]. No promise of a reply or an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps_emergency.title: We Make the Area Safe and Agree What Goes Up
steps_emergency.brief: The first stages of an emergency job from Table A: the area under the hazard closed off and access kept off it, the hazard and what can carry a scaffold looked at, and a safe interim arrangement chosen (a protective fan, edge protection, a scaffold that holds or takes down what is loose, a temporary roof where the job will run for weeks), with drawings where nothing standard covers it, said as what usually applies. The price for making it safe agreed before any work starts only from the price_agreed_before_work practice and [CV: quote_method]; what the permanent work costs waits until it has been seen. 'Same day' only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes. Never restates 'free'.

steps_emergency.title: We Put Up What Holds It Until the Repair
steps_emergency.brief: What usually happens: the interim scaffold built under supervision, handed over and checked before anyone uses it, then reviewed and altered or taken down once the permanent work allows (Table A). Wind, ice or a slippery roof can stop a safe build: say so, without a time. The roofer or builder who will work from it told what it is built for (Table E handover). Never promise a same visit build. Never mention the price.

Terms only from [CV: price_list]; adaptations as this business's practice only from the client values.

faq_slots.question: Do I need permission to put scaffolding up at my house?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the trade facts rule rows (Table C) and Table E and write what usually applies, with "usually" or "in most cases": a scaffold inside your own garden usually needs no permission while it serves work that is itself allowed; anything standing on or over the highway outside wants the council's permit first, which the scaffolder applies for in most cases, with lighting at night and a way past for people on foot as the usual conditions; one on next door's land needs their agreement; fixings into a listed building can need consent. problems.h2: The [WORK] Problems Every Job Is Planned Around

cards.title: Nowhere on the ground to build from
cards.brief: Access led, a situation and not a fault: the chimney sits on the ridge of a terrace with nothing under it but next door's roof, the gable is over a neighbour's extension, the back wall rises straight out of a conservatory or a lean to, the rear faces an alley a lorry cannot use. What decides it: what is directly below the work and whether it can take a scaffold's feet. What the work gives them, from Table A as what usually applies: a platform built off the slope of the roof, climbed to from an ordinary scaffold on the front or the back elevation (chimney scaffolding); a section that projects out from the building over the glass or the neighbour's side (cantilever and truss out); a bridged bay over what is in the way. Two readings in one card: the homeowner hears what will stand where and what it will touch; the roofer hears which arrangement it is and that a projecting or roof borne one is usually a drawn design rather than a standard arrangement (Table E), never the guidance's name. Never 'difficult access', never a symptom invented for it.
cards.mechanism: nothing under the work that can take a scaffold's feet

cards.title: The pavement, the road or next door in the way
cards.brief: Obligation led, written as normal steps and never as obstacles: the front door opens onto the pavement, the only way to the back is a shared side path, the gable is on the boundary, the flank wall is over next door's garden, the street is parked up. What decides it: whose land the feet stand on and what hangs out over it. What applies in most cases, from Table C and Table E: anything on or over the highway wants the council's permit first, which the scaffolder applies for as a rule, with lighting at night and a clear way past for people on foot as the normal conditions, and a parked bay suspended separately; on next door's land their agreement first, written down, and a party wall notice is not that agreement; the permit does not close a road. The homeowner reading: who asks whom, and that the licence date is usually the earliest the scaffold can go up. The trade reading: programme around the licence, not the other way. No fee, no lead time (Table G: none is national), never an Act's or a section's name.
cards.mechanism: feet or a platform on land that isn't the customer's

cards.title: A roof stripped with the weather coming
cards.brief: Protection led: write what the weather or a fall would do, why, and what prevents it. The situation: a re roof or a loft conversion that leaves the roof open for weeks, a long repointing job on a face above a path or a parked car, a flat roof with an open edge. The one cause this card makes: once the covering is off, nothing stands between the rain and the timbers and ceilings but what is put over them, and on an open face old mortar and offcuts fall on whoever is below (Table B temporary roofs, debris netting). What prevents it, from Table A: a temporary roof designed for its span and the wind with its covering kept up while the job runs; netting or sheeting on the face, told to the scaffolder before it goes on because a covered face catches the wind, which means more ties in most cases (Table E sheeting and wind); guard rails and toe boards at the edge. The homeowner reading: the rooms, the car and the path underneath. The trade reading: a sheeted or roofed scaffold is usually a designed one, so say so when the job is specified. Never a promise about the weather, never the guidance's name.
cards.mechanism: nothing between the weather and the timbers once the covering is off

cards.title: Every tile carried up a ladder
cards.brief: What slows a job down, from Table B hoists and loading bays and stair towers: materials carried up ladders by hand, nowhere to land a pallet of tiles, loads left on an ordinary working platform, several trades on one ladder all day. The one cause this card makes: the scaffold has no place made for materials to land and sit. What the work gives them, from Table A: a loading bay with a gate at the level the materials are used, a hoist where the loads warrant one, a stair tower where people are up and down all day. The trade reading: the loads and the trades told to the scaffolder when the job is specified, because a platform put up for one trade's work is not automatically up to another's loads (Table E handover). The homeowner reading: tiles and bags off the lawn and the drive, fewer trips past the windows. Never a load figure (the figures stay in the facts pack), never a safety lecture.
cards.mechanism: no place on the scaffold made for materials to land

cost.h2: What Moves the Price of an Emergency Call Out in [CITY]

cards.title: When you call
cards.brief: The time of day and the day of the week move the price: a Sunday evening against a weekday morning, a crew called back out against one already on its way to a job. A call out charge or an out of hours rate only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee] and [CV: price_list]; never say there is no charge for coming out unless [CV: quote_call_out_fee] says there is none. Whether the business comes out at those hours only from [CV: out_of_hours_available]; when it is not set, nothing about hours at all. Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: Getting there and getting it up
cards.brief: How far the job is from the yard and what is in the way once the lorry arrives: a scaffold that has to stand on a pavement with people kept past it, a parking bay to clear, a chimney over a neighbour's roof, a narrow lane with nowhere for the lorry to stand (Table F emergency scaffolding: restricted safe access, the public or the highway to keep clear). Distance and access move the price; say why in plain words. Never an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set; never hours of cover unless [CV: out_of_hours_available] says so.

cards.title: Closing it off and holding it
cards.brief: What is done first on a call out, from Table A emergency scaffolding: the area under the hazard closed off and people kept out of it, the loose masonry or the open roof edge and what can carry a scaffold looked at, then an interim arrangement chosen: a protective fan, a holding scaffold, a platform to take the loose piece down from. How much of that is needed, and whether anything standard covers it or it needs an urgent design (Table F: urgent bespoke design; Table E: a temporary roof is among the structures that normally need a design), is what the first part of the price pays for. Never how it is done beyond this.

cards.title: What's on the lorry and what has to follow
cards.brief: A first load of tube, boards and fittings comes with the crew; a bigger scaffold than that load, sheeting, a temporary roof or a stair tower means more brought from the yard, and a drawing where nothing standard covers it (Table A emergency scaffolding: a bespoke design where no standard configuration covers it). The hire runs under the contract from the day it goes up (Table E hire period), and the permanent scaffold for the repair, the alterations as the repair goes on and the licence where it stands on the pavement are priced as their own job (Table A: reviewed and altered or removed when the permanent work permits). Say what decides it and give no figure. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cards.title: Masonry loose over a path or a door
cards.brief: The situation from Table B emergency scaffolding: a chimney cracked by a gale, a parapet or a coping that has shifted, render coming off a gable above the front door, bricks loose above the pavement. The one cause this card makes: what is loose has only its own weight holding it, so the people under it are the risk before the building is. What usually happens when they call (Table A emergency scaffolding): the area underneath closed off first and kept closed, the hazard and what can carry a scaffold looked at, an interim arrangement put up under supervision (a protective fan over the path, a scaffold that holds the piece or lets it be taken down), handed over and checked, then altered or taken down once the repair is done. Both readings: the homeowner hears what will be closed and for how long only as the business says on the call; the builder hears what the interim scaffold is built for. Never a response time, round the clock cover or a call out promise unless [CV: response_time] or [CV: emergency_callouts] confirms it. Never that the building will fall down.
cards.mechanism: brick or stone with only its own weight holding it above the people below

cards.title: A roof opened by a storm or a fire
cards.brief: Tiles gone from a slope, a roof burnt through, a tree across the ridge, a chimney down through the covering. The one cause this card makes: the rooms below have nothing between them and the rain until something is put over them, and the roofer cannot work on it without an edge to stand behind (Table B temporary roofs, edge protection). What usually happens, from Table A: edge protection and a working platform for the roofer's first cover, or a temporary roof over the whole slope where the repair will run for weeks; wind can stop a safe build and that is said without a time. The trade reading: the roofer's dates and loads told to the scaffolder, because the interim scaffold is built for what was asked (Table E handover). The homeowner reading: whether the business deals with the home insurer only from the client values; what the policy needs is the insurer's to say (Table E: policies differ on telling the insurer about scaffolding). Never a promise about the weather.
cards.mechanism: the rooms below with nothing between them and the rain

cards.title: A scaffold that has moved or been hit
cards.brief: From Table B scaffold inspections and emergency scaffolding: a scaffold (anyone's) leaning after a gale, a lorry that has clipped a standard, sheeting torn and flogging in the wind, boards gone, a tie pulled out of the wall. The one cause this card makes: a base or a tie that has given, so the whole thing can shift. What usually happens, from Table A scaffold inspections: nobody on it and access kept off it until a competent person has looked at the feet, the ties, the boards and the guard rails and recorded what was found; a check after bad weather or anything that could affect it is what usually applies (Table E, the interval stays in the facts). The trade reading: the written record of the check. The homeowner reading: who to call when it is not their scaffolder's scaffold, only as the business says. Never a dig at the firm that put it up, never 'unsafe' as a verdict from the ground.
cards.mechanism: the whole scaffold shifting on a base or a tie that has given

cards.title: What to do before we get there
cards.brief: What the customer can do from the ground, from the trade facts first stage (make the area safe and keep people out of it): keep everyone, themselves included, from under what is loose; shut the gate, move the car, keep the children in, tell the neighbours whose path or garden is under it; where it is over the pavement, keep people walking past clear of it as far as that can be done without anyone standing under it; a photo from somewhere safe is useful to whoever repairs it and to an insurer. The one cause this card makes: every person who walks under it while they wait is the risk. Never a ladder, never anyone onto the roof or the scaffold, never an instruction to prop, tie or take anything down themselves; never a time by which anyone arrives unless [CV: response_time] is set.
cards.mechanism: people walking under what could still fall

faq_slots.answer_brief: Start with yes, then the terms from [CV: guarantee_years] and [CV: guarantee_scope]. Described, never promised.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for, named only as the client value gives it. Never what it pays or who it covers; never a legal minimum (Table E).

faq_slots.question: What happens if the scaffold damages something?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then the reasonable care and skill standard every trade works to. No promise to put it right free. Never invent a guarantee or an insurance outcome.

faq_slots.question: What happens when I ask for a quote in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: quote_method] and the confirmed practices only: what the customer sends, what the business looks at, what comes back. Where the town's streets put the scaffold on the pavement, the licence as a usual step before the start, without a lead time. No timescale unless [CV: response_time] is set.

faq_slots.question: Do you put scaffolding up all year round in [TOWN]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Yes, from Table A: the work runs all year, and what interrupts it is wind, ice and a roof too slippery to work on rather than a season; where the profile gives the town's exposure (a hilltop, a seafront), say what it does to a sheeted scaffold. No dates, no promise about the weather, nothing about busy times or booking ahead.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: The size of what's being inspected
cards.brief: A single lift on a semi against a scaffold round a whole block with several separate areas: the bigger and the more complex the structure, the longer each inspection takes and the more there is to record (Table F scaffold inspections: larger or more complex structure, more separate scaffold areas). Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: How often over the hire
cards.brief: How many inspections the hire needs: before first use, after a storm or an alteration, and at the interval the rules set for a construction scaffold, said as what applies and written only as the pack gives it (Table A; Table E construction scaffold inspection interval). A long hire with weather and changes means more visits than a short one (Table F: additional inspections after alterations or weather). No figure.

cards.title: A scaffold someone else built
cards.brief: An inspection of the business's own scaffold against one another firm put up: a stranger's scaffold means finding its design or its compliance sheet first, and a complex structure needs an inspector with the competence to match it (Table A: identify the structure and its design or compliance sheet; Table E: who inspects). Said without a dig at whoever built it; never that only the firm that built it may inspect.

cards.title: What the inspection finds
cards.brief: A clean report against one that records defects and the action they need: a loose tie, moved boards or torn sheeting leads to an alteration, priced as its own job, and the scaffold stays off limits until it is done (Table A: record defects and action, restrict unsafe access; Table B). The written report is what the rules ask for; a tag on the scaffold supplements it and does not replace it (Table E). Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

steps.title: Tell Us About the Scaffold
steps.brief: What to say: where it is, who built it, what it is for, how many lifts and how long it is staying up, and whether there is a design or a compliance sheet for it. The number from [CV: phone], the form only from [CV: quote_method].

steps.title: We Agree the Interval and the Price
steps.brief: What usually happens: the inspections the hire needs worked out from what the scaffold is and how long it stands, from the rules as the pack gives them (Table A; Table E), and the price for the visits from [CV: quote_method] and [CV: price_list] only. Never restates 'free'. No interval as a figure here.

steps.title: We Inspect, Record and Tag It
steps.brief: Each visit: the feet, the tube, the ties, the boards, the access and the guard rails looked at, what was found and what is to be done written up as the rules ask, the record left with the customer and the tag updated where one is used (Table A; Table E inspection record: the tag supplements the report). Anything unsafe kept off limits until it is put right. Never mention the price.

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: How far from a standard arrangement
cards.brief: A scaffold a standard compliance sheet already covers needs no design of its own; one with an unusual shape, a temporary roof, a cantilever over something or nowhere to put standard ties has to be calculated and drawn (Table A scaffold design: check the standard scope, calculate the non standard arrangement; Table E: a temporary roof is among the structures that normally need a design). Say it plainly and give no figure; never a guide's name as a selling point.

cards.title: What it has to carry
cards.brief: The loads on it: the trade's materials stacked on the platform, sheeting or netting that catches the wind, a hoist or a loading bay hung off it (Table E: sheeting and wind; the loading figure only as the pack gives it, never a class as a rule). The customer says what goes on it and the design is for that; a heavier use later means the design is looked at again (Table E handover).

cards.title: How many drawings and how many changes
cards.brief: One drawing for one arrangement against several interfaces with the building, revisions as the job changes, and a check of every proposed change before it is built (Table A: check proposed changes; Table F: multiple interfaces or revisions). Say why a change mid job costs design time again.

cards.title: The engineer's check
cards.brief: A design by a competent person with the calculation behind it is what the rules ask for; a check by an engineer where the client, the main contractor or the structure asks for one is a cost on top (Table E design responsibility: HSE does not say every design legally needs a chartered engineer, so never claim that it does). Said as what usually applies. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

steps.title: Tell Us About the Job
steps.brief: What to say: the building and what is being done to it, the shape of the scaffold wanted, what goes on it and for how long, the ground it stands on and what it can tie to, and whether anything goes over a pavement or a neighbour's land (Table A: obtain site, use, load and ground information). The number from [CV: phone], the form only from [CV: quote_method].

steps.title: We Draw It and Price the Design
steps.brief: What usually happens: the standard sheets checked first; where nothing covers it, the arrangement calculated, the bases, the bracing, the ties, the wind and the access specified and the drawings produced (Table A). The price for the design from [CV: quote_method] and [CV: price_list] only; the build priced as its own job. Never restates 'free'.

steps.title: We Issue the Drawings for the Build
steps.brief: The drawings and the instructions issued to whoever builds it, with what it is designed to carry; any change proposed on site goes back for a check before it is made (Table A: issue drawings and instructions, check proposed changes). Said without a time. Never mention the price.
